guard.fact_text: [L4] **$C^k$ calculus** ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]). A map $f$ is $C^k$ on an open set when every word of at most $k$ coordinate partial derivatives exists and is continuous; $C^\infty$ means $C^k$ for all $k$. Sums, scalar multiples and products of $C^k$ functions are $C^k$; a composition of $C^k$ maps is $C^k$; a map with continuous first partial derivatives everywhere on an open set is totally differentiable there, with derivative the Jacobian. Continuous functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable.
guard.quote:
Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

focused_proof_uses.text: 1.4 Let $f$ be continuous on the strip $B\times(-\delta,\delta)\times J$ (with $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ open, $\delta>0$) and suppose that every first partial derivative of $f$ exists and is continuous on each open half-strip $\{s>0\}$ and $\{s<0\}$ and extends continuously to the corresponding closed half-strip, the two extensions agreeing on $\{s=0\}$; let $E_i$ denote the resulting common continuous function on the whole strip, the index $i$ running over the four coordinates. Fix a point $p$ in the strip. If a segment $\beta\mapsto p+\beta e_i$, $\beta\in[0,h]$, stays inside one open half-strip, then $\beta\mapsto f(p+\beta e_i)$ is differentiable at every point of $[0,h]$ with derivative $E_i(p+\beta e_i)$ on $(0,h)$ and one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and $E_i$ is continuous, hence integrable, on $[0,h]$ [L4, L5]; the second fundamental theorem gives $f(p+he_i)-f(p)=\int_0^hE_i(p+\beta e_i)\,d\beta$. If the segment crosses $\{s=0\}$ at a parameter $\beta_0$, split the integral at $\beta_0$ and apply the same argument on the two closed subintervals, where the endpoint derivative at $\beta_0$ is the common one-sided value supplied by the continuous extension; additivity of the integral gives the same identity. If the segment lies entirely in the interface $s=0$ (a tangential or time direction), translate it by a positive normal distance $\epsilon$ and use the identity just proved on the positive half-strip. Continuity of $f$ and of $E_i$ on the compact translated-segment strip gives uniform convergence as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, hence the same integral identity on $s=0$. Dividing by $h$ and letting $h\to0$, continuity of $E_i$ at $p$ gives $(f(p+he_i)-f(p))/h=\tfrac1h\int_0^hE_i(p+\beta e_i)d\beta\to E_i(p)$; thus every first partial derivative of $f$ exists on the whole strip and equals the continuous function $E_i$. By [L4] $f$ is totally differentiable at every point with that Jacobian, and in particular all first partial derivatives are continuous, so $f$ is $C^1$ on the strip. [L4, L5, cases, algebra]

5.1 $\mathcal Ew$ is of class $C^\infty$ on each of the two open half-strips, with the following derivative formula on $s>0$, valid for every multi-index $\alpha$ and all $r,j\ge0$: $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kb_k^r\,\bigl[D_z^rD_y^\alpha\partial_\tau^j\bigl(\rho(z)w(y,z,\tau)\bigr)\bigr]_{z=b_ks},$ a finite sum for each fixed $(y,s,\tau)$ because only the finitely many $k$ with $|b_ks|<\delta/2$ contribute. On $s<0$ the function $\mathcal Ew$ equals $w$, which is smooth there. Both assertions follow by applying the product and chain rules [L4] termwise to a finite sum: on each set $\{s>\varepsilon\}$ with $\varepsilon>0$ the constraint $2^ks<\delta/2$ admits only finitely many $k$, so $\mathcal Ew$ is a finite sum of smooth functions there, and every point of $\{s>0\}$ has a neighbourhood with such an $\varepsilon>0$. Moreover, for every compact $Y'\times K\subseteq B\times J$ and all $\alpha,r,j$ there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,r,j}$, independent of $w$, with $\sup\{|D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)|:y\in Y',\,|s|<\delta/2,\,\tau\in K\}\le C_{\alpha,r,j}\sum_{|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\sum_{q\le r}\sup\{|D_y^\beta\partial_z^q\partial_\tau^jw(y,z,\tau)|:y\in Y'',\,-\delta/2\le z\le0,\,\tau\in K\}$ for some open $Y''$ with $Y'\subseteq\overline{Y''}\subseteq B$: each term contributes a factor $|a_k||b_k|^r$ times a fixed bound for the derivatives of $\rho$ of order at most $r$, and $\sum_k|a_k||b_k|^r<\infty$ by step 2.1. [step 2.1, step 4.1, L4, algebra]

6.1 For every multi-index $\alpha$, all $r,j\ge0$ and every compact $Y'\times K\subseteq B\times J$, the derivatives in step 5.1 converge uniformly as $s\downarrow0$ to $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$, and from the other side $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau)=D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,s,\tau)\to D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$. Indeed, choose an open $Y''$ with $Y'\subseteq\overline{Y''}\subseteq B$; all derivatives of $\rho w$ through order $r+|\alpha|+j$ appearing in step 5.1 are continuous on the compact set $\overline{Y''}\times[-\delta/2,0]\times K$, hence bounded by a finite constant $C$; the tail is bounded by $C\sum_{k>M}|a_k||b_k|^r\le576C\cdot2^{-M}$ by step 2.1, uniformly in $(y,s,\tau)$, while the finitely many head terms converge as $s\downarrow0$ because $\rho=1$ near $0$ and all positive-order derivatives of $\rho$ vanish at $0$, so each head term tends to $a_kb_k^rD_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$; the moment identity of step 3.1 makes the total limit equal to $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$, uniformly on $Y'\times K$. Consequently every mixed derivative of $\mathcal Ew$ on either side extends continuously to $s=0$, and the two one-sided continuous extensions agree there. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, L4, algebra]

9.1 By step 7.1 each $g_j$ with $j\ge1$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, and $g_0$ is $C^\infty$ by construction, so the finite sum $E_\Omega u$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ [L4]. Its derivatives on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ are the corresponding sums of the derivatives of the $g_j$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $j\ge0$ the boundary values on $\partial\Omega$ from the exterior side of the piece $g_i$ equal the corresponding boundary values of $\chi_iu$ by steps 6.1 and 7.1. [step 5.1, step 8.1, L4]

10.1 On $\Omega\times J$ one has $E_\Omega u=\sum_{j=0}^{p}\chi_ju=u$ because $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ there and each piece agrees with $\chi_ju$ on the physical side; by continuity this identity extends to $\overline\Omega\times J$. More generally, for every multi-index $\alpha$ and every $j\ge0$, the continuous extension of $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^ju$ to $\overline\Omega\times J$ equals $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)$ on $\overline\Omega\times J$: on the open set $\Omega\times J$ this is the Leibniz rule for the finite sum $\sum_i\chi_iu$ [L4], and on $\partial\Omega$ it follows from step 9.1 because the exterior boundary values of the pieces add up to the boundary values of $u$, the partition identity $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ holding on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. [step 8.1, step 9.1, L4, algebra]

focused_proof_uses.text: 2.1 The homogeneous blocks solve the wave equation with the prescribed data. Fix $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. By [F2] the function $H_\varphi(x,t)=t\,m_\varphi(x,ct,v_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Differentiating in $t$ and using the identity of step 1.2 at $s=ct$, one has $\partial_t^2H_\varphi=2c\,\partial_sm_\varphi+c^2t\,\partial_s^2m_\varphi$ and $c^2\Delta H_\varphi=c^2t\,\Delta m_\varphi=c^2t\,\partial_s^2m_\varphi+2c\,\partial_sm_\varphi$ for $t\ne0$; at $t=0$ both sides vanish, since $H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ gives $\Delta H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_sm_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ by evenness. Hence $\partial_t^2H_\varphi=c^2\Delta H_\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Differentiating this equation in $t$ and commuting $\partial_t$ with $\Delta$ through [F2] gives the homogeneous equation also for $K_\varphi:=\partial_tH_\varphi$; its data are $K_\varphi(\cdot,0)=\varphi$ by step 1.2 and $\partial_tK_\varphi(\cdot,0)=c^2\Delta H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F4]

7.1 Conclusion. Steps 2.2 and 4.1 show that $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense and that $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined; step 3.2 gives $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$, completing clause (a); clause (b) is step 5.1, clause (c) is step 5.2 and clause (d) is step 6.1. guard.fact_text: [L1] Radial Carleman lemma: for every integer $s\ge1$ with $\tau=s+1$ and every $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ compactly supported in an annulus $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, the weak Laplacian exists as a locally square integrable function and $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac2s\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_2$ ([[lem-three-dimensional-radial-carleman-integer-weight]]).
guard.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), in the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and put $\tau=s+1$. Write $r(x)=|x|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $\Delta$ be the Euclidean Laplacian ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Then for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $$\|r^{-\tau}u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}\le\frac{2}{s}\,\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}.$$ Moreover, if $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is compactly supported in an annulus $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, then the weak second derivatives of $u$ exist as locally square integrable functions, $\Delta u$ denotes their sum in the weak sense ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), and the same inequality holds for $u$. The weights $r^{-\tau}$ and $r^{-\tau+2}$ are bounded on every fixed compact annulus $\{a_0\le|x|\le b_0\}$ with $0<a_0\le b_0$, and this boundedness on the support of the function is the only property of the weights used in the density extension below; the weight $r^{-\tau}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge1$, and the weight $r^{-\tau+2}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge2$ and equals the constant $1$ for $s=1$. That is why the extension is stated for functions whose support stays away from $r=0$. The constant $2/s$ is explicit and is not claimed to be sharp.

focused_proof_uses.text: 2.1 **Carleman estimate with the potential split.** Let $M$ be the essential supremum of $|V|$ over $B_R(0)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure [L5]; it is finite because $B_R(0)$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$ and $V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and by [L5] one has $|V|\le M$ almost everywhere on $B_R(0)$. Applying [L1] to $u$ with parameter $s\ge1$, $\tau=s+1$, and using $|V|\le M$ together with $r\le R$ on the support of $u$, one has $\|r^{-\tau+2}Vu\|_2\le MR^2\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2$ and therefore $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac2s\bigl(MR^2\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2+\|r^{-\tau+2}e\|_2\bigr)$. [L1, L5, step 1.1]

Its s>=2 clause refers only to whether r^(-tau+2) is unbounded at the origin; it explicitly equals1 for s=1. Consumer L1/step2.1 uses the allowed inequality with the annular localization of1.1; AComega is assumed in the consumer Statement/Given/Choice accounting. Later absorption retains s>=max{1,4MR²}. focused_proof_uses.text: 3.3 **Termwise differentiation.** Each degree term $x\mapsto r^{-l-1}\int|y|^lP_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy=\int\rho(y)|x|^{-l-1}P_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))\,dy$ is harmonic on $\{|x|>a\}$ because the coefficient kernel of [L1] is harmonic in $x$ and smooth jointly in $x$ and $y$ on observation compact sets times $\overline B_a(0)$, with $y=0$ read by its homogeneous polynomial extension. Its derivatives through order two are uniformly bounded there. Multiplying their uniform difference-quotient bounds by $|\rho|$ and integrating, [L9] identifies the derivatives of the integral with the integrals of the derivatives; therefore its Laplacian is the integral of zero. This justifies harmonicity of each integrated term, rather than treating an integral as a finite sum. Let $K$ be compact with $\inf_K|x|=r_1>a$, choose $a<r_2<r_1$ and a compact neighbourhood $K'$ of $K$ contained in $\{|x|>r_2\}$. The partial sums $S_N(x)=\sum_{l\le N}(\text{degree-}l\text{ term})$ are harmonic on $\{|x|>a\}$, and by step 2.1 they converge uniformly on $K'$; applying the interior derivative estimates [L8] to $S_M-S_N$ on $K'$ for each multi-index $\alpha$ gives $\sup_K|D^\alpha(S_M-S_N)|\to0$, so the differentiated series converges uniformly on $K$ for every $\alpha$. Since $S_N\to F$ pointwise and the first derivatives converge uniformly on $K$, the Newton–Leibniz theorem [L9] applied along coordinate segments identifies the limit of $\partial_iS_N$ with $\partial_iF$ on $K$; inductively the same identification holds for every order, so the series may be differentiated termwise to every order on $K$ and $F$ is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$ in the sense of [L10]. [L1, L8, L9, L10, step 2.1]

guard.fact_text: [L1] $c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}\ge a^{2}>0$ for every $s$, and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with $\frac{d}{dt}\sqrt t=\frac{1}{2\sqrt t}=\frac12t^{-1/2}$; general power derivatives and continuity are as in [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]. ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]])
guard.quote:
Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

focused_proof_uses.text: 1.1 Smoothness and speed (a). The map $s\mapsto c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}$ is a polynomial, hence $C^\infty$, with values in $[a^{2},\infty)\subseteq(0,\infty)$; by [L1] the square root is $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$, so the composite $s\mapsto\sqrt{c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}}$ is $C^\infty$ and $z$ is $C^\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ [L2]. Its derivative is $z'(s)=(c^{2}s/\sqrt{c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}},0,0)$ by the chain rule [L1, L2], so $|z'(s)|=c^{2}|s|/\sqrt{c^{2}s^{2}+a^{2}}$ [L2]. If $s=0$ this is $0<c$; if $s\ne0$, dividing numerator and denominator by $c|s|>0$ gives $|z'(s)|=c/\sqrt{1+a^{2}/(c^{2}s^{2})}<c$ because $a^{2}/(c^{2}s^{2})>0$ [L3]. Hence $|z'(s)|<c$ for every $s$. [given, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphism.full_cited_section:
Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

lem-three-dimensional-radial-carleman-in.full_cited_section: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), in the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and put $\tau=s+1$. Write $r(x)=|x|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $\Delta$ be the Euclidean Laplacian ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Then for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $$\|r^{-\tau}u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}\le\frac{2}{s}\,\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}.$$ Moreover, if $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is compactly supported in an annulus $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, then the weak second derivatives of $u$ exist as locally square integrable functions, $\Delta u$ denotes their sum in the weak sense ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), and the same inequality holds for $u$. The weights $r^{-\tau}$ and $r^{-\tau+2}$ are bounded on every fixed compact annulus $\{a_0\le|x|\le b_0\}$ with $0<a_0\le b_0$, and this boundedness on the support of the function is the only property of the weights used in the density extension below; the weight $r^{-\tau}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge1$, and the weight $r^{-\tau+2}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge2$ and equals the constant $1$ for $s=1$. That is why the extension is stated for functions whose support stays away from $r=0$. The constant $2/s$ is explicit and is not claimed to be sharp.

thm-of-square-roots.full_cited_section:
Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.
